sections.title: What "AI skills" means in job descriptions

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Cloud services and AI libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

"AI skills" rarely means building neural networks. For a Java full stack developer it usually means two things: using AI tools to work faster and safely, and building features on top of models using normal engineering.

| Level | What it means | Who needs it | Your priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| AI-assisted development | Generate, review, test and debug with tools such as Copilot or Claude Code | Almost every developer | Must have |
| AI application engineering | Call LLM APIs, RAG, tools and agents from Spring | Many backend and full stack roles | Your differentiator |
| AI in production | Evaluation, security, cost, observability | Teams shipping AI features | Know the essentials |
| Machine learning engineering | Train models, statistics, PyTorch, GPUs | Specialist ML roles | Not needed |

A small sample of 2026 postings asks for LLMs, RAG, vector databases and AI APIs, for Java libraries such as Spring AI and LangChain4j, and for use of copilots. Many of those roles are senior or contract, so treat it as a direction rather than a requirement for fresher jobs. For a fresher, it is a way to stand out.

### What you do not need to know first

You do not need calculus or backpropagation to integrate an LLM, just as you don't need compiler theory to write Java. You do need a working mental model of how models behave, which is the rest of this part.

### How this shows up in interviews

| Question | What they are checking |
|---|---|
| How do you use AI tools? | You are productive and critical: you review and test output |
| Add a chatbot over our documents | RAG design, citations, access control, cost |
| How do you stop it inventing answers? | Grounding, evaluation, allowing "I don't know" |
| How do you know it works? | Evaluation sets, not a few manual tries |
| What could go wrong? | Prompt injection, data leakage, cost, latency |
Say "I built a RAG feature in my project and evaluated it on 40 questions" rather than claiming production AI experience. It sounds stronger, and it survives follow-up questions.
blocks.title: Be honest about experience
Key points
blocks.text:
- You do not need to train models
- AI tool use is becoming a baseline
- Integrating LLMs is backend engineering
- One shipped feature beats many courses

A large language model predicts the next piece of text, given the text so far. Everything surprising about LLMs follows from that.

### Tokens

Models do not read words. Text is split into **tokens**, which are common chunks of characters. As a rough rule for English, one token is about three-quarters of a word. Tokens are the unit of cost and limits, so a 1,000-word document is around 1,300 tokens. Languages, code and unusual strings tokenise differently, and it's why LLMs can miscount letters: they don't see letters directly.

### Generation, one token at a time

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Your prompt] --> B[Split into tokens]
  B --> C[Model scores every possible next token]
  C --> D[Sampling picks one]
  D --> E[Append to the text]
  E --> F{End or limit?}
  F -->|no| C
  F -->|yes| G[Response]
blocks.title: What happens inside one call

blocks.text:
Training adjusted billions of numbers so that this prediction works well. The model has absorbed patterns from a huge amount of text, but it has no database of facts to look up. This explains why it can write well about a subject and still state something false with full confidence.

### Context window

The **context window** is the most tokens that a model can consider in one request: your instructions, the history, retrieved documents and its own answer together. Anything beyond the limit must be trimmed. More context also costs more and can distract the model, so choosing what to send is a core engineering skill.

### The model is stateless

The API does not remember your last request. A "conversation" is an illusion created by resending the history each time, which is why long chats get more expensive per message. Memory is your code's job.

### Parameters

| Parameter | Effect | Use |
|---|---|---|
| temperature | Randomness in choosing tokens | Low for extraction, higher for creative text |
| max tokens | Upper limit on the answer | Control cost, avoid runaway output |
| top-p | Limits choices to likely tokens | Usually adjust this or temperature, not both |
| stop sequences | End generation when seen | Structured formats |

Even at temperature 0, outputs are not guaranteed to be identical across calls or model versions. Do not build logic that needs exact text.

### Why models hallucinate

A model always produces plausible next tokens, even when it has no real knowledge. It may invent a method name in a library, because it looks like what such a method would be called. Mitigations: give it the source text (RAG), ask for citations, allow "I don't know", validate outputs in code, and never let it be the only check on something important.

### Choosing a model

Providers offer several sizes. Larger models reason better, cost more and respond more slowly. Small ones are often enough for classification or extraction. Pick by testing against your own evaluation set, not by benchmarks. Model names change often, so keep the model name in configuration.

**"Why does the same prompt give different answers?"** Generation samples from probabilities, and temperature controls how much. So I test against an evaluation set, validate structured outputs in code, and keep logic independent of exact wording.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Models predict tokens, they do not look up facts
- Tokens are the unit of cost and limits
- The model is stateless
- Confident does not mean correct

An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers (a **vector**) so that similar meanings land close together. "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login" share few words, but their vectors are close. This powers semantic search and RAG.

### Measuring closeness

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. Values near 1 mean very similar meaning. You rarely compute it by hand, as the database does it, but the idea matters.

blocks.title: Embedding text with Spring AI

blocks.text:
### Things to get right

- **Use one model for everything in an index.** Vectors from different models are not comparable. Changing model means re-embedding all your documents.
- **Dimensions** must match your database column. Many models use hundreds to a few thousand.
- **Embeddings miss exact identifiers.** Codes such as `ERR-4021` are poorly captured, so combine with keyword search.
- **Beyond search:** you can use embeddings for grouping, recommendations and duplicate detection.

### Nearest-neighbour search

Comparing a query with every vector is exact but slow at scale. Databases use **approximate** indexes, such as HNSW, which are much faster but may miss a few results. You tune the balance of speed and recall.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Vectors place similar meanings close together
- Keep one embedding model per index
- Exact codes need keyword search too
- Approximate indexes trade some recall for speed

sections.title: Inside the model: an intuitive tour

blocks.text:
You do not need the maths, but a working picture of the internals helps you predict behaviour, and it comes up in interviews.

### From words to numbers

Each token becomes a vector of numbers, which is its embedding inside the model. During training, tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors. A classic illustration is that the direction from "king" to "queen" resembles the direction from "man" to "woman".

### Attention: what the transformer added

Consider: "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because **it** was too big." To understand "it", you must look back at "trophy". Earlier models read text in order, and struggled to carry meaning across long distances. The **transformer** architecture, introduced in 2017, lets each token look at every other token and decide how much each one matters. This mechanism is called **attention**.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Tokens] --> B[Embeddings plus position]
  B --> C[Attention layers: tokens exchange information]
  C --> D[Scores for every possible next token]
  D --> E[Sampling picks one]
  E -->|appended| A
blocks.title: A simplified transformer pipeline

blocks.text:
Attention compares tokens with each other, so processing grows with text length, which is one reason longer context costs more time and money.

### How a model is trained

| Stage | What happens | Why it matters to you |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-training | Predict the next token over a huge amount of text | Creates general knowledge, up to a cutoff date |
| Tuning on instructions | Learn from examples of good responses | Makes it follow requests rather than simply continue text |
| Safety training | Learn to decline harmful requests | Explains some refusals |

Three consequences follow. The model has a **knowledge cutoff**, so anything later needs to be supplied. It learned from examples of how text *usually* continues, so it writes plausible text whether or not it's true. And it's not updated by your conversations, as training is a separate, expensive process.

### Why some tasks are surprisingly hard

| Task | Why it's hard | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Counting letters | Tokens hide individual letters | Use code |
| Big arithmetic | Predicting digits isn't calculating | Provide a calculator tool |
| Today's date or prices | Beyond the cutoff | Provide it in the prompt, or a tool |
| Quoting exact text | Paraphrase is more natural | Retrieve it, and verify in code |
| Very long lists | Attention and output limits | Split the work |

The general rule is to give the model what it's bad at through tools, and use it for what it's good at: language, summarising, classifying, and drafting.

### Reasoning models

Some models spend extra tokens thinking before answering, which improves multi-step problems at a higher cost and latency. For straightforward extraction they waste money, so test whether a given task actually benefits.

### Fine-tuning, RAG or prompting?

| Need | Best first choice |
|---|---|
| Follow your format or tone | Prompt with examples |
| Answer from your documents | RAG |
| Fresh or user-specific data | Tools |
| Consistent specialised style at high volume | Fine-tuning, usually later |

Fine-tuning changes behaviour rather than adding reliable facts, and it brings a dataset, a process and costs. Most application developers rarely need it.

### Running models yourself

Open-weight models can run on your own GPUs, or through Ollama on a laptop, and Spring AI supports them. This may suit strict privacy needs, or very high steady volume. Don't underestimate the costs of GPUs, operations and generally lower quality. A hosted API is usually the right start.

**"How does an LLM work, in a minute?"** Text is split into tokens and converted to vectors. Layers of attention let each token use context from the others, producing a score for every possible next token. One is sampled, appended, and the process repeats. Training set the weights by predicting text at huge scale, so the model is great at plausible language but has no built-in check for truth.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Attention lets tokens use distant context
- Knowledge stops at a cutoff
- Use tools for maths, dates and fresh data
- Prompt first, then RAG, and fine-tuning last

Interviewers increasingly ask about this, and it's where a backend developer can stand out.

### A cost model

blocks.code:
cost per call = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price
monthly cost  = calls per day × 30 × cost per call
blocks.title: The formula, for one feature

blocks.text:
### A worked example

Prices below are **made up for arithmetic**. Always check the provider's current price page. Suppose a model costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens.

A support assistant handles 5,000 questions a day, with these prompt parts:

| Part | Tokens |
|---|---|
| System instructions | 400 |
| Retrieved chunks (5 × 300) | 1,500 |
| History | 600 |
| Question | 100 |
| **Input total** | **2,600** |
| Answer (output) | 300 |

Per call: 2,600 × $3/1,000,000 = $0.0078 for input, and 300 × $15/1,000,000 = $0.0045 for output, so $0.0123.

Per month: 5,000 × 30 × $0.0123 = **$1,845**.

### What changes the bill

| Change | New cost per call | Saving |
|---|---|---|
| Retrieve 3 chunks, not 5 | 2,000 input: $0.0105 | 15% |
| Trim history to 200 tokens | 2,200 input: $0.0111 | 10% |
| Shorter answers, 150 tokens | $0.0078 + $0.00225 = $0.0101 | 18% |
| Model at one-fifth of the price | $0.00246 | 80% |

Model choice dominates, which is why **routing** pays off: a small model for simple questions, and a larger one for the hard ones. But measure quality before switching.

### Capacity and rate limits

Providers limit requests and tokens per minute. Check peak rather than average: if 5,000 daily questions concentrate into 8 busy hours, with a peak of three times average, that's about 31 calls a minute, or about 90,000 tokens a minute. Compare this with your account's limits, and plan for a queue.

### Concurrency in your service

If each call takes 8 seconds, then 31 calls a minute means about 4 in flight at a time on average, and more during bursts. This is Little's law: **in-flight = arrival rate × duration**. It tells you what bulkhead size and thread count to set.

### Per-user limits

blocks.title: Reject before spending money

blocks.text: Without limits, one script or abusive user can spend your monthly budget overnight. Add a global daily budget alert too.
About four characters per token for English works for planning. Use the provider's counting API, or the usage field in responses, for real numbers.
blocks.title: Rough token estimate
Key points
blocks.text:
- Multiply tokens by price, per part of the prompt
- Model choice dominates the bill
- Plan for peak, not average
- Limit each user before spending money

sections.title: What really goes over the wire

blocks.text:
Frameworks hide the HTTP call, which is convenient until something breaks. Understanding the raw request makes every framework easier to debug. Providers differ in details, but the shape is similar. Check your provider's API reference for exact fields.

### A request

blocks.title: A typical chat request (shape varies by provider)

blocks.text:
The whole conversation is in each request. This is what "stateless" means in practice. The model's previous reply has to be sent back by you, and in principle you could edit it, which shows that nothing is stored on the model's side unless a provider adds a feature for it.

### A response

Check the stop reason:

| Stop reason (names vary) | Means | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Normal end | Finished | Use it |
| Max tokens | Cut off | JSON may be broken; raise the limit or continue |
| Tool use | Wants a tool | Run it, and send the result |
| Content filter or refusal | Blocked | Handle separately |

A truncated JSON answer is a classic production bug, so check this before parsing.

### Calling it from plain Java

blocks.title: A minimal client with RestClient

blocks.text:
Header names and paths are provider-specific. Writing this once, as an exercise, teaches you what `ChatClient` does for you.

### Streaming on the wire

Streaming uses server-sent events: an open HTTP response, with chunks arriving as text.

blocks.title: Part of a streamed response (shape varies)

blocks.text:
Proxies can break this. If your text arrives in one big lump at the end, something in the path is buffering. Check Nginx's `proxy_buffering`, and the settings of any load balancer or gateway. Idle timeouts can also cut long pauses, so send keep-alive comments.

### Tool calling on the wire

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Your app
  participant M as Model
  A->>M: messages + tools list with JSON schemas
  M-->>A: stop reason: tool use, name orderStatus, input {"orderId":42}
  A->>A: run the function
  A->>M: all previous messages + the tool call + the tool result
  M-->>A: final text
blocks.title: The messages in a tool call

blocks.text:
Every tool's name, description and schema is sent in each request, so it counts as input tokens. That's why 200 tools are expensive before any work begins.

### Errors to handle

| Status | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | Bad request, or context too long | Don't retry; trim or fix |
| 401, 403 | Key or permissions | Don't retry; alert |
| 408, 5xx | Provider trouble | Retry with backoff |
| 429 | Rate limited | Respect `Retry-After`; slow down |
| Overloaded (often 503 or 529) | Temporary | Retry, or fall back to another model |

Don't retry a request after a long timeout without thought: the provider may have completed it, and you pay again.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The whole conversation goes in each request
- Check the stop reason before parsing
- Tools add input tokens to each call
- Only retry transient errors

Amazon Bedrock provides models from several companies through one AWS API. For companies already on AWS, this often passes security review more easily than a new external vendor.

### Why teams choose it

| Benefit | Details |
|---|---|
| IAM, not API keys | Tasks use their role |
| Private network paths | VPC endpoints |
| One bill and one contract | Fits existing procurement |
| Several model providers | Switch with little code change |
| Data handling terms | Check the current terms for your use |

The trade-offs: newest models may arrive later than on the maker's own API, model availability differs by Region, and you need to request or enable access to models.

### Using it from Spring AI

blocks.title: Region and model; credentials come from the task role

blocks.text: Your `ChatClient` code doesn't change, which is the benefit of the abstraction. Don't set access keys in properties: use the default credentials chain. The Converse API doesn't cover embeddings, so these use a separate Bedrock embedding model starter. Check which models and Regions are currently supported in Spring AI's documentation and the AWS console.

### Managed extras

| Feature | What it does | Consider when |
|---|---|---|
| Guardrails | Filters for content, personal data and denied topics | You want a managed layer |
| Knowledge Bases | Managed RAG: ingestion, chunking, retrieval | You want speed over control |
| Agents | Managed tool-calling loop | Simple workflows |
| Prompt caching | Cheaper repeated prefixes | Large stable instructions |
| Batch | Discounted offline work | Non-urgent bulk jobs |

Managed RAG gets you started quickly, but you lose fine control over chunking and evaluation. Building it yourself, as in Part 4, teaches far more, and interviews expect you to understand what's inside.

### Hosting your own model

SageMaker or GPU instances can serve open-weight models. A rough check: a GPU instance runs all day, whether busy or idle, whereas API calls cost nothing when idle. So hosting only pays off at high, steady volume, or with strict requirements. Include the cost of the people to run it.

### Choosing

| Situation | Reasonable choice |
|---|---|
| Learning or a personal project | The cheapest direct API with a budget limit |
| Company on AWS with strict security | Bedrock |
| Need a provider's newest features at once | Direct API |
| Strict data residency, high volume | Evaluate self-hosting |

**"How would you call an LLM from a Spring Boot service on ECS, securely?"** Through Bedrock, using the task role instead of API keys, over a VPC endpoint. Model ID in configuration, timeouts and limits in code, and only the permitted models allowed in IAM.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Bedrock gives many models through one AWS API
- Use IAM rather than keys
- The ChatClient code stays the same
- Self-hosting pays only at high, steady volume
#### What "AI skills" means in job descriptions

items.question: Do you need Python for AI application roles in Java?
items.answer: Not for integration work, since Spring AI and LangChain4j cover it. Reading basic Python helps, as many examples use it, and dedicated AI teams may require it.

items.question: What separates an AI engineer from an ML engineer?
items.answer: An AI application engineer builds products on existing models. An ML engineer trains and optimises models.

blocks.text: #### How an LLM produces text

items.question: Why does a long chat cost more per message?
items.answer: The model is stateless, so the whole history is resent every time, and you pay for those tokens. Trim or summarise it.

items.question: A model invented a library method. Why?
items.answer: It predicts plausible text, and that name looks plausible. It has no check against the real library. Give it the docs, then compile and test.

items.question: When would you use low temperature?
items.answer: When consistency matters, such as extraction and classification.

blocks.text: #### Embeddings and similarity

items.question: You switch embedding models. What must you do?
items.answer: Re-embed all stored documents. Vectors from different models cannot be compared.

items.question: Why might semantic search miss the product code X-204?
items.answer: Embeddings capture meaning, and rarely capture exact codes. Hybrid search adds keyword matching.

blocks.text: #### Inside the model: an intuitive tour

items.question: Why can't a model tell you today's news on its own?
items.answer: Its knowledge stops at its training cutoff. Provide fresh data through a tool or retrieval.

items.question: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to teach a model your product's facts?
items.answer: It shapes behaviour, rather than reliably storing facts, and it goes stale. RAG can be updated and cited.

items.question: Why give a model a calculator tool?
items.answer: It predicts digits rather than calculating, so big arithmetic can be wrong. Code gives an exact answer.

blocks.text: #### Estimating cost and capacity

items.question: Requests take 10 seconds, and you get 60 a minute. How many are in flight?
items.answer: Little's law: 1 request per second × 10 seconds = about 10 concurrently.

items.question: Which change usually saves the most money?
items.answer: Using a smaller model where quality allows, then reducing context.

items.question: Why check the token limit at peak rather than the daily total?
items.answer: Limits apply per minute, so a busy hour can hit them even though the daily total looks small.

blocks.text: #### What really goes over the wire

items.question: JSON parsing fails on some long answers only. What's the likely cause?
items.answer: The output hit the max tokens limit and was cut off. Check the stop reason, and raise the limit or reduce the output.

items.question: Text only appears at the end, even though you're streaming. Why?
items.answer: A proxy in the path is buffering the response. Turn off buffering there.

items.question: Why might 200 tools be costly even when none is used?
items.answer: Their definitions are sent as input tokens on each request.

blocks.text: #### AI on AWS: Bedrock

items.question: Why might a security team prefer Bedrock?
items.answer: IAM access control, private endpoints, one vendor contract, and logs within AWS, with no new API keys.

items.question: What does Spring AI's abstraction give you when moving to Bedrock?
items.answer: ChatClient code stays the same. Only the dependency and configuration change, although behaviour should be re-evaluated.

items.question: When is hosting your own GPU model sensible?
items.answer: At high, steady volume, or with strict requirements that managed services can't meet, after counting staffing costs.
